transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, what brings me in is that my eating has just gotten really off. Some days I... I barely get down a cup of coffee and a granola bar before my shift. And my scrubs have been hanging pretty loose on me lately, even though I'm not trying to lose any weight at all. I just haven't been eating much.
Over this same period when your eating has decreased, how has your mood been? Have you been feeling sad, down, or empty most days?

Yeah, I have been feeling pretty down. Most mornings I wake up with this... heavy, hollow feeling. It just feels like the day is already ruined before I even put on my badge for work. So, yeah, I'd say empty is a good word for it.
Have you experienced periods like this before—times when your mood was down, you weren't eating well, and you felt this heavy, empty feeling?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days here and there, like anyone, but... not like this. This heavy feeling and the weight loss, it's all new to me. I haven't really dealt with anything quite like this before.
How long have you been experiencing this heavy, empty feeling and the changes in your eating?

Well, it's been a while. The steady depression and... just the loss of interest in eating and everything else, that settled in a bit later on. I'd say it's been with me for roughly the past year and four months now.

Before this past year and four months, have you ever had a period of time—even a few weeks or months—where you felt depressed, had no appetite, and felt that same heavy, empty feeling, and then it went away completely before this current episode started?

No, like I said, I haven't really dealt with anything like this before. Before this past year or so, I never had a time where I felt this down or lost my appetite like this. It's all just been since this started.
Besides the changes in eating, have you noticed any changes in your sleep? Are you sleeping more, less, or about the same as usual?

I'm definitely sleeping less. My sleep is... it's just broken up. I'll lie there at night, just replaying everything from work in my head, and... I keep listening for noises. And then, even when I do fall asleep, I end up waking up around 3 or 4 in the morning. After that, I just can't settle back down before my alarm goes off. So, yeah, I'm not getting much rest.

You mentioned that this heavy feeling and loss of appetite started about a year and four months ago. Did something specific happen around that time—an event at work, a loss, an accident, or something traumatic—that seemed to trigger when all of this began?

Well, yeah, it kind of did. The clinic where I work, they did this huge overhaul of the electronic medical records system and completely changed the workflow. That meant my hours got all shifted around. It was a really stressful time. That was almost two years ago now, and that's when this whole thing really started.
Since the workflow changes at your clinic almost two years ago, has your mood and these symptoms stayed pretty much the same the whole time, or have they gotten better or worse at different points?

I'm not really sure if there were specific points where it got better or worse. It feels like... well, it's just been pretty much the same this whole time. I haven't really noticed it lifting or changing much. It's just been a steady drag since all those changes happened at work.

When the electronic medical records system changed at your clinic almost two years ago, did your mood and appetite problems start right away—like within days or weeks—or did they develop more gradually over a longer period of time?

It didn't all hit me at once, no. At first, it was just the stress of the new system and the schedule changes. But the actual... that steady, heavy feeling, the depression, and just not caring about food or anything else... that settled in a bit later. I'd say that part has been with me for roughly the past year and four months.

When you think back to those first few months after the schedule and system changes started—before the heavy feeling and depression settled in—how were you coping with the stress of those changes? Were you managing okay, or were you already struggling emotionally right from the start?

Well, I wasn't really managing it well, no. I was struggling, but just... differently at first. A few months after they made all those shift changes—I guess that would be about a year and eight months ago—that's when I started hearing voices. And I also started getting this sense that people were sending me signs through the new schedule. So, yeah, that was all happening before the heavy, depressed feeling really took over.

When you started hearing voices about a year and eight months ago, were you already feeling that heavy, empty, depressed feeling at that time, or did the depression come later after the voices started?

The depression definitely came later. Actually, um, there was even a period back then when my mood had eased up enough that I was running a little bit again, you know, just getting through the day okay. But even during that time—for several weeks—I was still hearing those comments when I walked down empty hallways at the clinic. And I kept reading the work schedule like it had these hidden warnings specifically about me. So, my mood was actually okay for a bit, but those other things were already happening before the heavy feeling really hit.
Are you still hearing those voices in the hallways at work right now, or have they stopped?

Yeah, I'm still hearing them. It's usually when I'm walking down the hallway or when I'm near the phlebotomy room and nobody else is around. I'll hear my name, or just short comments, like... like someone saying "he messed up again." And it still happens even on days when I'm not feeling particularly sad or heavy.

Besides hearing those voices and feeling like the schedule has hidden messages about you, do you believe that other people—maybe coworkers or people outside of work—are deliberately trying to harm you, control you, or send you messages in other ways?

Well, I don't really think people outside of work are doing anything. But at the clinic... yeah. I just keep getting stuck on this idea that certain people there are watching my charting times. Like they're tracking exactly when I log my notes. And I feel like they're leaving these little signs in the schedule just to show me that they're building a case against me. I've brought it up, and my supervisor tells me it's just the new workflow and nobody's doing that, but... I don't know, I just can't shake the feeling that they are.

During that period when you were running a bit and getting through the day okay—before the heavy, depressed feeling hit—did you notice anything unusual about your energy level, your need for sleep, or how many projects or goals you were taking on at work or at home?

No, not really. Um, my energy was just pretty normal during that time. I wasn't staying up late or feeling like I didn't need to sleep, and I definitely wasn't taking on any extra projects at the clinic or at home. I was just going to work, doing my shifts, and coming home. The running was just my regular routine, nothing extreme. I just felt... normal, I guess, before the depression really set in.

Looking back over your entire life before this past year and a half—say, in your teens or twenties—have you ever had a period lasting a week or more where you felt unusually energized, needed much less sleep than normal, and were taking on a lot of projects or activities at once?

No, I don't think so. Um, I've never really been the type to have endless energy or go without sleep. Even back in my teens and twenties, I pretty much just stuck to my normal routine. I've always needed a regular amount of sleep to get by, so... no, I've never had a week like that where I was just taking on a bunch of things at once. I've always just been pretty steady in that regard.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a 16-month history of persistent depressive symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia, appetite loss, sleep disturbance) that developed following an initial psychotic episode approximately 20 months ago. The psychotic features include auditory hallucinations (hearing voices in empty hallways at work) and delusions of reference (believing the work schedule contains hidden messages about him and that coworkers are monitoring and building a case against him). Critically, the psychotic symptoms persist independently of mood state—the patient explicitly reports hearing voices even on days when not feeling particularly sad. The temporal sequence shows psychotic symptoms emerging first (approximately 20 months ago), followed by a period of mood recovery with persistent psychosis, and then the onset of sustained depressive symptoms (16 months ago) that have remained relatively stable. The absence of any manic episodes, the primary prominence of psychotic symptoms that occur both during and outside depressive periods, and the chronic course support a diagnosis of schizophrenia rather than a primary mood disorder.
